claims.text: Preferential Cu enrichment at the nanoparticle surface induces a liquid skin that governs the onset and progression of premelting and melting.
The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are initially solid and have homogeneous bulk composition and unmodified surface chemistry.
A thin oxide or sulfur capping layer can suppress Cu segregation in FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles.
Surface treatment will produce an inhibited Cu segregation profile relative to untreated nanoparticles.
Cu has a lower melting point than the other relevant alloy constituents.
The lower melting point of Cu promotes its segregation to the nanoparticle surface.
Surface-segregated Cu forms a liquid-like surface layer during heating.
The Cu-rich liquid-like layer locally lowers the melting barrier.
The liquid surface layer propagates inward and triggers a cascade of localized premelting events.
Suppressing Cu segregation causes nanoparticles to require higher temperatures to initiate melting.
Untreated nanoparticles will develop liquid-like surface regions and other premelting features at lower temperatures than capped nanoparticles.
The phase-transformation onset temperature will be lower in untreated nanoparticles than in treated nanoparticles.
Melting will progress faster in untreated nanoparticles than in treated nanoparticles.
Surface-treated nanoparticles define a homogeneous-surface baseline and show delayed premelting relative to untreated particles.
Sluggish diffusion kinetics and multicomponent interactions may limit Cu segregation and its effect on the local melting barrier.
Equivalent Cu distributions in treated and untreated batches would falsify the proposed Cu-segregation mechanism.

contradictions.description: The boundary field correctly states that equivalent Cu concentrations would indicate failure of the surface treatment and confound causal attribution, whereas the falsification rule treats equivalent Cu distributions as falsification. A failed manipulation does not test whether successfully suppressing Cu segregation changes melting.
